An ISS astronaut controls a robot on Earth?

And again, I know you don't realize the magnitude, the significance of this human "master" in space, controlling a robot on earth -- but it is really breathtaking. One more link in the chain that marches ever closer to robot interdependence, and the next great step, this time on the shoulders of robots. Ah -- it was fun while it lasted, right?

Imagine this robot was on Mars rather than on Earth. And instead of the astronauts being on the ISS, they're in a station or parked spacecraft in Mars orbit or maybe on Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos. Almost all the work of construction in space in the future is going to be done by telerobots. Humans will never do the heavy-lifting in space.

So if you're building a permanent settlement on Mars, some significant construction that's going to take some years, it's possibly more practical to put your 'builders' shed' in orbit than on the surface because the supplies overhead and necessary systems reliability factors for shuttling humans back and forth from the surface is very high, making the expense very high. Until a comprehensive ISRU (in-situ resource utilization) capability is established on the surface, the resource overhead to support humans is about the same, but more expensive to put on the ground than in orbit. Whether you're sitting at a teleoperation console in a prefab habitat nearby, in orbit, or in an office building on Earth, it's all the same work. The only difference is the telecommunications latency and how much on-board robot intelligence you can effectively use to compensate. If you're doing things via an Earth to Mars link, work is going to be really slow or your robots need to be very smart and independent. If that level of intelligence seems unlikely, then you need people to operate them from a closer distance. Mars orbit would be close enough that the latency would be modest while still being cheaper than sending people to the surface.

Of course, there's still the 'space wasting' issue. The debilitation that takes place after extended exposure to microgravity. We still don't have any viable clinical solution to that. It will be a major feat for astronauts to get to Mars without being very debilitated by the time they arrive. If they must stay for years more in microgravity in orbit, and then on the trip back, it may not be survivable. But we don't really know that their fate would be all that much better on Mars either. There is a common supposition that Mars' reduced gravity is enough to minimize this effect to where it can be compensated for simply by exercise and such. We don't really know. There's no way to simulate Mars gravity for very long periods.

This is why, in the late '70s and '80s, the idea of giant orbital colonies became popular, supplanting the planetary settlement ideas of the Wernher von Braun era. Space medicine wasn't looking very promising then and a lot of space-futurists thought that these giant colonies might be the only practical way for human beings to live off the Earth. But the pharaonic scale of these projects made them untenable, or at least implausible in the eyes of the public. Even experimenting with rotating gravity structures was beyond what post-Space Race NASA could hope to do with the meager funds allotted them. All these years and no one has actually done even a modest space experiment for this.

I tend to be bullish on the eventuality of a clinical solution, but given how things are going it might be moot. Space may ultimately belong to machines and transhumanists.
